Abstract Cocculus hirsutus is a widely used herb in traditional systems of medicine for the treatment of various diseases. In the present study, five alkaloids (1–5), two flavonoids (6–7), one triterpenoid (8), and three steroids (9–10) were isolated from the roots of Cocculus hirsutus and further crude extract was analyzed by LC-Q-Tof-MS/MS in positive ionization mode leading to the identification of ten metabolites through comparison of exact molecular masses from their MS/MS spectra, mass fragmentation studies and with literature data. In addition, a method was developed and validated for the quantification of four bio-active compounds [Sinococuline (1), Magnoflorine (2), (E)-N-feruloyltyramine (3), and 20-Hydroxyecdysone (10)] using UPLC-QqQ-MS in multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode for the first time. The method has shown good linearity with correlation coefficients (r2) higher than 0.9916 for all four compounds. The intra- and inter-day precision were in the range of 0.3–6.1% and from 0.7% to 8.8%, respectively. The matrix effects of all the four analytes were found in the range of 94.7 ± 2.8–112.7 ± 3.7%. Overall, our study provides a reliable and rapid approach by hyphenated LC-MS/MS using high-resolution mass spectrometers for identification and quantification of bioactive constituents from the root extracts of Cocculus hirsutus. Keywords Cocculus hirsutus ; Extraction optimization ; Chemical profiling ; Simultaneous quantification ; UPLC-QToF-MSe and UPLC-QqQ-MS-MRM Introduction Cocculus hirsutus (Linn.) Diels (family: Menispermiacae) is a well-known traditional medicinal plant popularly known as “patalagarudi” in Ayurveda. It is a climber, commonly found across the tropical and subtropical climates of Asian countries including India [1], [2], [3]. Every part of this plant is used in indigenous systems of medicine, the people in tropical and sub-tropical regions of countries made preparations from this plant for treatment of a wide variety of ailments including diarrhea, jaundice, bronchitis, anorexia, and leprosy [4]. A decoction made from dried leaf, and stem parts of the plant have been used in the treatment of eczema, dysentery, eye disease and urinary infections. The extracts from roots extracts were reported for several health benefits such as antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, spermatogenic, antibacterial, and antioxidant activities [5], [6]. In previous studies, triterpenoids, flavonoids (quercetin) and alkaloids have been identified from the aerial parts and roots of C. hirsutus. Recently, aqueous extract from the stem of C. hirsutus (AQCH) was examined for dengue activity [7], [8] which showed potent activities and further fingerprint analysis of these active extracts indicated markers, sinococuline, magnoflorine, 20-hydroxyecdysone, coniferyl alcohol and makisterone, respectively. It is well known fact that, establishing the best quality control by identification and quantification of representative active markers in the herbal preparation is a major challenge [9]. Although, few analytical techniques have been reported for the chemical analysis of C. hirsutus, such as GC-MS for volatiles [10], LC-MS for active compounds [11], and LC-MS/MS for bioanalytical analysis of sinococuline [12], but identification and quantification of bioactive markers were still unclear. No quantitative method has been reported for the simultaneous analysis of major bioactive constituents from the roots of C. hirsutus as to control the quality and safety of C. hirsutus, variations in these bioactive markers can be considered as essential quality indicators. In the present study, a unique LC-QTof-MS based approach was developed to identify metabolites from the optimized extract of C. hirsutus along with quantification of major bioactive constituents using UPLC-QqQ-MS. The developed approach can be used as a quality control parameter to assess the quality of Cocculus hirsutus products, and also provides a basis for quality assurance in the large scale production of herbal preparations and their clinical application in the future. W.Theob. (Menispermaceae) is a perennial climber distributed mostly in tropical and subtropical areas. The main aim of this article is to collect and analyze the scientific information related to traditional uses, bioactive chemical constituents and pharmacological activities. Methods: Scientific information on C. hirsutus was retrieved from the online bibliographic databases (e.g. MEDLINE/PubMed, SciFinder, Web of Science, Google Scholar and Scopus). Information regarding traditional uses was also acquired from secondary resources including books and proceedings. Results: Different plant parts of C. hirsutus were reported to be used for the treatment of fever, skin diseases, stomach disorders and urinary diseases. Alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives along with a few flavonoids, triterpene derivatives and volatile compounds were reported from whole plant or different plant parts. Extracts were evaluated for their antimicrobial, antidiabetic, immunomodulatory and hepatoprotective activities among others. Conclusion: Although widely used in traditional medicines, only a few studies have been performed related to chemical constituents. Most of the biological activity evaluations were carried out using in vitro evaluation methods and only a few studies were carried out in animal models. In the future, properly designed in vivo and clinical studies are necessary to evaluate the pharmacological activities of C. hirsutus along with bioassay-guided studies to isolate and identify the active constituents. Introduction The Menispermaceae family consists of about 70 genera and 500 species [1]. Among them, the genus Cocculus comprises about 10 species distributed in Asia, Africa, Australia and North America [1]. Cocculus hirsutus (L.) W.Theob (Figure 1) (syn. Cebatha hirsuta (L.) Kuntze, Cebatha villosa C.Chr., Cocculus aristolochiae DC., Cocculus hastatus DC., Cocculus hirsutus (L.) Diels, Cocculus holopeira-torrida Broun & R.L.Massey, Cocculus linnaeanus Kurz, Cocculus sepium Colebr., Cocculus villosus DC., Menispermum hirsutum L.) [2] is a perennial climber distributed mostly in tropical and subtropical areas [3]. In Asia, it is reported from India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan and southern China [1,4,5,6]. In Africa, it is reported from Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea, Angola and south-west and southern Africa [1,6]. The detailed distribution in Asia and Africa is given in Figure 2 [7]. It is known by various names in local languages such as: Broom creeper (English); Huyer (Bengali); Farid buti, Jamti ki bel (Hindi); Kaage Mari (Kannada); Farid buti (Urdu); Paathaalagarudakkoti (Malayalam), Kaanse laharo (Nepali); Garudi, Patalagarudi (Sanskrit), Chipuru-tiga (Telegu); Kattu-k-koti (Tamil) among others [3,4,8]. Various plant parts of C. hirsutus are widely used in South Asia for the treatment of fever, rheumatism, skin disorders and visceral diseases and also as a detoxifier [9]. In Africa, stems are used to make baskets and the purple berries are eaten or used to dye basket materials. Leaves are used by Tsonga people as an important herb in their diet [1]. Regarding the pharmacological activity evaluations, extracts obtained from the plant parts of C. hirsutus have shown potent diuretic, laxative [10], analgesic and anti-inflammatory activities [11]. Mainly alkaloids and some other compounds are reported from whole plant or different plant parts, however the detailed chemical analysis has not been performed yet. A current pandemic outbreak of Coronavirus diseases-2019 (COVID-19) has affected 216 countries and territories and more than 47 million cases were reported till 3 November 2020 (https://www.worldometers.info/coronavirus/). Along with the research on the development of vaccines and antiviral drugs, many researchers are also focusing on the plant-derived natural products as potential sources of therapeutic agents. According to Clinical Trials Registry-India [12], an open label, randomized, comparative, multi-center, parallel group, controlled clinical study has been started in India to evaluate the effect and safety of aqueous extract of Cocculus hirsutus (AQCH) tablets in treatment of Coronavirus infection (CTRI Number: CTRI/2020/05/025397, registered on 28 May 2020). Previously, a randomized, Phase-I, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation study to evaluate safety and tolerability of AQCH tablets in healthy adult human subjects was registered (CTRI Number: CTRI/2019/12/022297, registered on 10 December 2019). To the best of our knowledge, the outcomes of these studies have not been published yet. For a medicinal plant species that has been widely used in traditional medicines and is also being considered as a source for the development of therapeutic agents for various diseases, it is important to critically analyze and understand the available scientific information about the chemical constituents and pharmacological activities. Thus, the aim of this article is to compile and analyze the available scientific information about these reported aspects of C. hirsutus. fetched_contents.text: Phytochemical Screening and GC-MS Analysis of Methanolic and Aqueous Extracts of Ocimum kilimandscharicum Leaves Abstract Kenyans have long utilized Ocimum kilimandscharicum, an East African permanent evergreen plant, to treat measles, stomachaches, diarrhea, mosquito bites (anti-insect), congested chest, cough, and colds. Using conventional qualitative and quantitative techniques, this study was done to identify the secondary metabolites in O. kilimandscharicum leaf extracts. The chemical content of the crude extracts from the leaves of O. kilimandscharicum has also been investigated and characterized using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS). By using a 1:20 dilution in methanol, in cold maceration, a fine powder of O. kilimandscharicum was first extracted then filtered and concentrated after 72 h utilizing a rotary evaporator. By using also a 1:20 dilution in water at 80 °C, a fine powder of O. kilimandscharicum was extracted and then filtrated and lyophilized 1 h later. Each extract underwent further gas chromatography–mass spectrometry testing. We found that both extracts contain secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins. However, the overall amount of phytochemicals in each solvent varied significantly. Total phenolics contents (TPCs) were 5.6 ± 1.20 and 10.8 ± 1.00 mg, total flavonoid contents (TFCs) were 8.2 ± 0.4 and 39.6 ± 2.2 mg, total tannin contents (TTCs) were 0 ± 0.00 and 10.5 ± 0.4 mg, the total alkaloid content (TAC) was 49.2 ± 0.40%, and the total saponin content (TSC) was 38 ± 2.00%. Additionally the gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, revealed a number of high- and low-molecular-weight bioactive molecules at various concentrations for each extract. We also found an inhibitory effect on adhP and chbR gene expression of Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella choleraesuius, respectively. Hence, these chemicals could potentially have a biological and pharmacological significance. Therefore, the discovery of many physiologically active chemicals in the leaf extracts of O. kilimandscharicum justifies future biological and pharmaceutical research. 1. Introduction Traditional medicines are defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as knowledge, skills, and practices that vary across cultures and are used to treat or prevent physical or mental illnesses based on theories, first-person experiences, and beliefs.1 Phytochemicals or active secondary metabolites are abundant in medicinal plants and are widely used in traditional medicine. Only 2% of the known medicinal plants’ species (350,659) in the world are scientifically investigated for their phytochemical constituents and beneficial bioactivities.2,3 Population growth, insufficient drug supply, rising treatment costs, side effects of several synthetic drugs, and the development of resistance to drugs have all contributed to a greater emphasis on the use of plant materials as a source of medicine for a wide range of human ailments. Drugs originating from natural resources play an important role in both traditional and contemporary medical systems4,5 The World Health Organization (WHO) has taken appropriate efforts to conduct research with the goal of discovering novel and effective therapeutic compounds from plants.6 Among the many traditionally important plants, the genus Ocimum sp. is well-known worldwide and have been used for thousands of years due to its diverse medicinal properties.7 The genus diversity carries more than 150 individual species. The growth preferences of these plants are mostly located in the tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, Africa, and Central and South America. Many Ocimum sp. were investigated for their medicinal properties and use of crude extracts. Specifically, the insecticidal, fungistatic, and antibacterial properties of the plant extracts are well-documented.8,9 From the Ocimum genus, Ocimum kilimandscharicum, commonly known as camphor basil, is native to Eastern Africa. This species has been extensively used in traditional medicine to cure colds, coughs, malaria, stomach discomfort, and diarrhea.10 Additionally, O. kilimandscharicum is a commercially important fragrant enhancer for cosmetics.16 Few studies have reported certain biologically active components of O. kilimandscharicum from varieties growing in Asia.11 However, the phytochemical profiling of the East African O. kilimandscharicum is still sparse, although its insecticidal and medicinal properties have been documented.12,13 Currently, comprehensive phytochemical profiling has been done only on few species of the Ocimum genus.14 Additionally, agroecological conditions and cultivation practices could significantly affect the phytochemical profile between plants from different agroclimatic areas.15 Hence, the characterization of the phytochemicals that are present in O. kilimandscharicum cultivated in East Africa (Kenya) needs to be done because of its clinical and medical importance. To date, numerous extraction, separation, purification, and quantification procedures have been used to identify phytochemicals from medicinal plants. Reported chemical compounds and classes in Cocculus hirsutus

The evidence points to several major compound classes commonly reported in Cocculus hirsutus studies, with alkaloids being the most consistently named. The review explicitly states that “alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives” are among the most commonly reported constituents, along with some flavonoids, triterpene derivatives, and volatile compounds [N3-R1]. The review also notes that previous studies have identified triterpenoids, flavonoids (including quercetin), and alkaloids from the aerial parts and roots of C. hirsutus [N3-R2]. A broader phytochemical summary similarly lists alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, and glycosides as important phytochemicals reported from Cocculus species [N4-R2], although this is not Cocculus hirsutus-specific.

For specific compounds, the evidence is mixed. The most directly named compounds come from a 2023 review and a 2023 chemical profiling study: five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids were isolated from the roots of Cocculus hirsutus, with explicit examples including sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone [N1-F1]. Another source also reports isolated compounds such as 2-hexyldecanoic acid and a complex flavonoid-like structure, but these appear to be from a different Cocculus hirsutus study rather than the most commonly repeated ones [N1-R5]. The review notes that “many studies have reported the preliminary phytochemical screening of the extracts and presence of carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, [and] ...” [N4-R1], which is a broad but less specific listing.

Methods used to identify compounds differ by technique. The 2023 chemical profiling study is a strong example of more rigorous compound identification: it uses LC-QTof-MS/MS and UPLC-QqQ-MS, identifies 25 metabolites, and quantifies four major bioactive compounds [N1-F1]. In contrast, GC-MS is used in a separate Cocculus hirsutus source to report compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2]. Another source reports chloroform extract of Cocculus hirsutus containing 15 compounds, 11 of which are nitrogenous compounds [N1-R3]. A phytochemical screening source also states that preliminary screening can detect carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and similar classes [N4-R1]. The evidence therefore shows a pattern: GC-MS is used for volatile/semi-volatile compounds and simpler compound classes, whereas phytochemical screening and more advanced LC-MS/MS are used for broader class detection and more specific compound identification [N1-F1][N1-R2][N2-F3].

Overall, the most commonly reported classes in Cocculus hirsutus studies are alkaloids, flavonoids, triterpenoids, steroids, and volatile/semi-volatile compounds, with GC-MS contributing to the identification of some of the more volatile compounds, while phytochemical screening and LC-MS/MS provide broader class-level evidence [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence also suggests that the compound list is not fully standardized across studies, and some sources report only class-level findings rather than specific named compounds [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Methodological context for compound identification

Phytochemical screening methods in the evidence are described as qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling techniques. One source explicitly says that phytochemical screening includes qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling of ethnomedicinal plant species [N2-R2]. Another source describes a study using water and methanol extraction coupled with gas chromatographic methods to identify biologically active compounds [N2-F3]. The methodological emphasis is on detecting secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins, but the same source notes that the overall amount of phytochemicals varied significantly across solvent extracts [N2-F3].

GC-MS contributes by enabling identification of volatile and semi-volatile metabolites, including fatty acids, amines, esters, and other small molecular-weight compounds [N2-R3]. A separate study on Ocimum kilimandscharicum further illustrates that GC-MS can reveal high- and low-molecular-weight bioactive molecules at various concentrations in extracts [N2-F3]. In Cocculus hirsutus, GC-MS has been used to report specific compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], which aligns with the idea that GC-MS is best suited for volatile/semi-volatile compounds rather than large, non-volatile metabolites. The evidence also shows that GC-MS is often used in combination with other methods, such as qualitative phytochemical screening, which can detect broader classes like alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3][N2-R4].

Limitations are clear. First, phytochemical screening is typically class-level and qualitative, so it may overstate presence without identifying specific compounds [N2-R2][N2-F3]. Second, GC-MS is limited by its sensitivity to volatility and molecular weight; it may miss polar, non-volatile, or thermally unstable compounds [N2-R3]. Third, the evidence shows that different solvent extracts can yield very different phytochemical profiles, which means a single extract may not represent the whole chemical composition [N2-F3]. Finally, the review notes that most of the available chemical information for Cocculus hirsutus is limited, suggesting that findings may not be fully comparable across studies [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These methodological differences explain why some sources report only class-level constituents and others report specific compounds: phytochemical screening and GC-MS are complementary but not equivalent methods for compound identification [N2-R2][N2-R3][N1-F1].

Species-specific and comparative evidence

The evidence suggests that Cocculus hirsutus findings are partly consistent across studies but also species-specific or at least genus-specific. The review states that different plant parts of C. hirsutus were reported to be used for fever, skin diseases, stomach disorders, and urinary diseases, and that “alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives” were among the most commonly reported constituents [N3-R1]. It also notes that previous studies have reported triterpenoids, flavonoids, and alkaloids from the aerial parts and roots of C. hirsutus [N3-R2]. This implies some consistency in the major classes reported for C. hirsutus.

However, the same review also says that “only a few studies have been performed related to chemical constituents” and that “detailed chemical analysis has not been performed yet” [N3-R2][N3-F2]. A more recent chemical profiling study isolated five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids from the roots, with explicit named compounds including sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone [N1-F1]. This suggests that the most detailed chemical characterization comes from a specific study on roots, not from general or broad reports on the genus. The evidence therefore supports the view that Cocculus hirsutus findings can be species-specific and part of a broader Cocculus genus pattern, but the genus-level evidence is not fully resolved.

Comparative evidence is limited but informative. A Cocculus species review notes that Cocculus species contain various bioactive molecules in different concentrations, with Cocculus species containing more phenolic compounds than alkaloids [N4-R3]. Another source reports phytochemical analysis of “both species” and lists alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, etc. [N4-R2]. A separate review on Cocculus hirsutus also reports that chloroform extracts of C. hirsutus contain alkaloids, saponins, phenolic compounds, and other phytochemicals [N4-R5]. These sources suggest that Cocculus species share some common classes, but the exact compounds and concentrations may differ across species.

Conflicting or incomplete findings matter because the evidence is uneven. Some sources report broad classes and some report named compounds, while others note limited or incomplete chemical analysis [N3-R2][N3-F2][N4-R5]. The review explicitly states that most biological activity evaluations were carried out using in vitro methods and that few studies were carried out in animal models, with only limited chemical analysis available [N3-F2]. This means that reported compounds may not be fully validated across all studies, and conclusions about Cocculus hirsutus should be cautious about overgeneralizing beyond the specific methods and extracts used [N3-F2][N4-R5].

Compound classes and nomenclature evidence

The evidence shows that several compound classes are most often named across the sources, with alkaloids appearing most frequently. The Cocculus hirsutus review lists “alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives” as among the most commonly reported constituents [N3-R1]. It also reports flavonoids, triterpene derivatives, and volatile compounds [N3-R1]. A broader phytochemical summary similarly lists alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, and glycosides as important phytochemicals reported from Cocculus species [N4-R2]. Another source reports secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins in plant extracts [N2-F3], while a GC-MS source identifies volatile/semi-volatile metabolites such as fatty acids, amines, esters, etc. [N2-R3].

Phytochemical reports and chemical identification reports overlap but differ in scope. Phytochemical reports tend to be broader and often class-level, identifying the presence of alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, saponins, tannins, etc., without necessarily naming specific compounds [N2-R2][N2-F3][N4-R2]. Chemical identification reports, by contrast, can name specific compounds and sometimes isolate them, as in the Cocculus hirsutus study that isolated five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids, with named examples such as sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone [N1-F1]. GC-MS reports also often name specific compounds, such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], while other sources describe compounds as nitrogenous or high- and low-molecular-weight bioactive molecules without full nomenclature [N1-R3][N2-F3].

Nomenclature ambiguity affects interpretation because the same class can be reported in different ways. A source states that phytochemical screening is used to identify the class of phytochemicals such as flavonoids, carotenoids, phenols, polyphenols, glycosides, tannins, etc., but does not always resolve the exact compound name [N2-R5]. This means that “flavonoid” may refer to a broad class rather than a single compound, and “alkaloid” may refer to a group of compounds rather than a single named molecule. The evidence also shows that some studies report named compounds while others only report classes, which makes comparisons across sources difficult [N2-R5][N2-F3][N1-F1]. In short, the overlap between phytochemical reports and chemical identification reports is real, but the nomenclature ambiguity means that compound reports should be interpreted cautiously and should not be assumed to be fully equivalent across sources [N2-R2][N2-R5][N1-F1].

## 1) What the evidence says about compounds and classes

The available evidence indicates that Cocculus hirsutus has been reported to contain several major compound classes, with alkaloids being the most consistently named and frequently emphasized. The review explicitly states that “alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives” are among the most commonly reported constituents, along with some flavonoids, triterpene derivatives, and volatile compounds [N3-R1]. ## 2) Which methods were used and what they typically detect

The methods used to identify compounds in Cocculus hirsutus differ by technique and resolution:

- **Phytochemical screening** is described as qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling [N2-R2]. It is typically used to detect broad classes such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3]. The review also notes that preliminary phytochemical screening can detect carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and similar classes [N4-R1].
- **GC-MS** is used to identify volatile/semi-volatile metabolites, including fatty acids, amines, esters, and other small molecular-weight compounds [N2-R3]. In Cocculus hirsutus, it has been used to report compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], and to identify nitrogenous and other bioactive compounds in extracts [N1-R3].
- More advanced **LC-MS/MS** and **UPLC-QqQ-MS** are used for more precise compound identification and quantification, as shown by a recent Cocculus hirsutus study that identified 25 metabolites and quantified four major bioactive compounds [N1-F1].

## 3) What compound classes are most often named and how they overlap

Across the sources, the most often named compound classes are:

- **Alkaloids** – the most consistently emphasized class, including jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine, and their derivatives [N3-R1], and more specifically sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone in one study [N1-F1].
- **Flavonoids** – reported in multiple Cocculus hirsutus and Cocculus species sources, often as a class or as specific examples such as quercetin [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Triterpenoids** – mentioned in both Cocculus hirsutus and broader Cocculus species evidence [N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Steroids** – reported in Cocculus hirsutus studies and phytochemical summaries [N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Phenolics, phenols, saponins, tannins** – common in phytochemical reports and often detected by GC-MS or phytochemical screening [N2-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2].
- **Volatile/semi-volatile compounds** – specifically highlighted by GC-MS as the class best suited to this method [N2-R3].
- **Nitrogenous compounds** – reported in chloroform extract of Cocculus hirsutus [N1-R3].

These classes overlap substantially across sources, but the overlap is not always exact. Phytochemical reports often name classes broadly, while chemical identification reports can name specific compounds. GC-MS reports can also name specific compounds, but they are more often associated with volatile/semi-volatile classes [N2-R3][N1-R2][N1-F1].

## 4) How phytochemical reports differ from chemical identification reports

Phytochemical reports and chemical identification reports differ mainly in scope and specificity:

- **Phytochemical reports** are usually qualitative or semi-quantitative and often focus on class-level detection. They are described as chemical class profiling techniques [N2-R2], and they commonly identify broad classes such as alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, glycosides, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3][N4-R2][N4-R1].
- **Chemical identification reports** are more specific and often include named compounds, isolation data, and quantitative methods. The Cocculus hirsutus study that isolated five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids, with named examples such as sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone, is a clear example of this approach [N1-F1].
- **GC-MS reports** can bridge these two approaches: they can name specific compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], but they are also often used to detect broader volatile/semi-volatile classes [N2-R3].

Nomenclature ambiguity is a major issue because the same class name can be used differently across sources. The review also notes that previous studies have identified triterpenoids, flavonoids (including quercetin), and alkaloids from the aerial parts and roots of C. hirsutus [N3-R2]. A broader phytochemical summary similarly lists alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, and glycosides as important phytochemicals reported from Cocculus species [N4-R2], although this is not Cocculus hirsutus-specific.

For specific compounds, the evidence is mixed. The most directly named compounds come from a 2023 review and a 2023 chemical profiling study: five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids were isolated from the roots of Cocculus hirsutus, with explicit examples including sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone [N1-F1]. Another source also reports isolated compounds such as 2-hexyldecanoic acid and a complex flavonoid-like structure, but these appear to be from a different Cocculus hirsutus study rather than the most commonly repeated ones [N1-R5]. The review notes that “many studies have reported the preliminary phytochemical screening of the extracts and presence of carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, [and] ...” [N4-R1], which is a broad but less specific listing.

The 2023 chemical profiling study is a strong example of more rigorous compound identification: it uses LC-QTof-MS/MS and UPLC-QqQ-MS, identifies 25 metabolites, and quantifies four major bioactive compounds [N1-F1]. In contrast, GC-MS is used in a separate Cocculus hirsutus source to report compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2]. Another source reports chloroform extract of Cocculus hirsutus containing 15 compounds, 11 of which are nitrogenous compounds [N1-R3]. A phytochemical screening source also states that preliminary screening can detect carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and similar classes [N4-R1]. Overall, the most commonly reported classes in Cocculus hirsutus studies are alkaloids, flavonoids, triterpenoids, steroids, and volatile/semi-volatile compounds, with GC-MS contributing to the identification of some of the more volatile compounds, while phytochemical screening and LC-MS/MS provide broader class-level evidence [N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-F1][N1-R2]. Methodological context for compound identification

Phytochemical screening methods in the evidence are described as qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling techniques. One source explicitly says that phytochemical screening includes qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling of ethnomedicinal plant species [N2-R2]. Another source describes a study using water and methanol extraction coupled with gas chromatographic methods to identify biologically active compounds [N2-F3]. The methodological emphasis is on detecting secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins, but the same source notes that the overall amount of phytochemicals varied significantly across solvent extracts [N2-F3].

GC-MS contributes by enabling identification of volatile and semi-volatile metabolites, including fatty acids, amines, esters, and other small molecular-weight compounds [N2-R3]. A separate study on Ocimum kilimandscharicum further illustrates that GC-MS can reveal high- and low-molecular-weight bioactive molecules at various concentrations in extracts [N2-F3]. In Cocculus hirsutus, GC-MS has been used to report specific compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], which aligns with the idea that GC-MS is best suited for volatile/semi-volatile compounds rather than large, non-volatile metabolites. The evidence also shows that GC-MS is often used in combination with other methods, such as qualitative phytochemical screening, which can detect broader classes like alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3][N2-R4].

Limitations are clear. First, phytochemical screening is typically class-level and qualitative, so it may overstate presence without identifying specific compounds [N2-R2][N2-F3]. Second, GC-MS is limited by its sensitivity to volatility and molecular weight; it may miss polar, non-volatile, or thermally unstable compounds [N2-R3]. Third, the evidence shows that different solvent extracts can yield very different phytochemical profiles, which means a single extract may not represent the whole chemical composition [N2-F3]. Finally, the review notes that most of the available chemical information for Cocculus hirsutus is limited, suggesting that findings may not be fully comparable across studies [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These methodological differences explain why some sources report only class-level constituents and others report specific compounds: phytochemical screening and GC-MS are complementary but not equivalent methods for compound identification [N2-R2][N2-R3][N1-F1].

Integrated final answer on compounds and classes identified in Cocculus hirsutus

## 1) What the evidence says about compounds and classes

The available evidence indicates that Cocculus hirsutus has been reported to contain several major compound classes, with alkaloids being the most consistently named and frequently emphasized. The review explicitly states that “alkaloids such as jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine and their derivatives” are among the most commonly reported constituents, along with some flavonoids, triterpene derivatives, and volatile compounds [N3-R1]. Another review notes that previous studies have identified triterpenoids, flavonoids (including quercetin), and alkaloids from the aerial parts and roots of C. hirsutus [N3-R2]. A broader phytochemical summary similarly lists alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, and glycosides as important phytochemicals reported from Cocculus species [N4-R2].

For specific compounds, the evidence is more uneven. The most directly named compounds come from a recent chemical profiling study, which isolated five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids from the roots of Cocculus hirsutus, with examples including sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone [N1-F1]. A different Cocculus hirsutus source also reports isolated compounds such as 2-hexyldecanoic acid and a complex flavonoid-like structure, but these appear to be from a separate study rather than the most commonly repeated ones [N1-R5]. A GC-MS source reports caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol in Cocculus hirsutus [N1-R2], while another source notes that chloroform extract of Cocculus hirsutus contains 15 compounds, 11 of which are nitrogenous compounds [N1-R3].

## 2) Which methods were used and what they typically detect

The methods used to identify compounds in Cocculus hirsutus differ by technique and resolution:

- **Phytochemical screening** is described as qualitative and quantitative chemical class profiling [N2-R2]. It is typically used to detect broad classes such as alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3]. The review also notes that preliminary phytochemical screening can detect carbohydrates, steroids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and similar classes [N4-R1].
- **GC-MS** is used to identify volatile/semi-volatile metabolites, including fatty acids, amines, esters, and other small molecular-weight compounds [N2-R3]. In Cocculus hirsutus, it has been used to report compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], and to identify nitrogenous and other bioactive compounds in extracts [N1-R3].
- More advanced **LC-MS/MS** and **UPLC-QqQ-MS** are used for more precise compound identification and quantification, as shown by a recent Cocculus hirsutus study that identified 25 metabolites and quantified four major bioactive compounds [N1-F1].

## 3) What compound classes are most often named and how they overlap

Across the sources, the most often named compound classes are:

- **Alkaloids** – the most consistently emphasized class, including jasminitine, hirsutine, cohirsitine, and their derivatives [N3-R1], and more specifically sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone in one study [N1-F1].
- **Flavonoids** – reported in multiple Cocculus hirsutus and Cocculus species sources, often as a class or as specific examples such as quercetin [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Triterpenoids** – mentioned in both Cocculus hirsutus and broader Cocculus species evidence [N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Steroids** – reported in Cocculus hirsutus studies and phytochemical summaries [N3-R2][N4-R2].
- **Phenolics, phenols, saponins, tannins** – common in phytochemical reports and often detected by GC-MS or phytochemical screening [N2-F3][N4-R1][N4-R2].
- **Volatile/semi-volatile compounds** – specifically highlighted by GC-MS as the class best suited to this method [N2-R3].
- **Nitrogenous compounds** – reported in chloroform extract of Cocculus hirsutus [N1-R3].

These classes overlap substantially across sources, but the overlap is not always exact. Phytochemical reports often name classes broadly, while chemical identification reports can name specific compounds. GC-MS reports can also name specific compounds, but they are more often associated with volatile/semi-volatile classes [N2-R3][N1-R2][N1-F1].

## 4) How phytochemical reports differ from chemical identification reports

Phytochemical reports and chemical identification reports differ mainly in scope and specificity:

- **Phytochemical reports** are usually qualitative or semi-quantitative and often focus on class-level detection. They are described as chemical class profiling techniques [N2-R2], and they commonly identify broad classes such as alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, phenols, sterols, glycosides, saponins, and tannins [N2-F3][N4-R2][N4-R1].
- **Chemical identification reports** are more specific and often include named compounds, isolation data, and quantitative methods. The Cocculus hirsutus study that isolated five alkaloids, two flavonoids, one triterpenoid, and three steroids, with named examples such as sinococuline, magnoflorine, and 20-hydroxyecdysone, is a clear example of this approach [N1-F1].
- **GC-MS reports** can bridge these two approaches: they can name specific compounds such as caryophyllene, α-humulene, and eugenol [N1-R2], but they are also often used to detect broader volatile/semi-volatile classes [N2-R3].

Nomenclature ambiguity is a major issue because the same class name can be used differently across sources. The evidence also shows that some studies report named compounds, while others only report classes. This means that a source reporting “alkaloids” may not necessarily have identified the same named alkaloid as another source, and a GC-MS report naming a specific compound may not be fully comparable to a phytochemical report that only identifies a class [N2-R5][N2-F3][N1-F1]. Because of this, compound reports should be interpreted cautiously and should not be assumed to be fully equivalent across sources [N2-R5][N2-F3].
